5bbbad529ebe0f613b39acf5cae841fc71ab9d26.answer:
The pit lane speed limit is 80 km/h for the whole competition [1]. The Race Director may amend this limit to ensure the safe and orderly conduct of the competition [1].

Drivers who exceed the limit during free practice, qualifying, or sprint qualifying are fined €100 for each km/h over the limit, up to a maximum of €1000 [1]. During a TTCS, the stewards may instead impose a 5-second, 10-second, drive-through, or stop-and-go penalty [1].

aa69721830619d61b35cae1ff52395057a62c763.answer:
The speed limit in the Pit Lane is 80 km/h during the whole Competition. However, to ensure the safe and orderly conduct of the Competition, the Race Director may amend this limit [1].

When leaving the grid, all drivers must respect the Pit Lane speed limit until they pass pole position [2][3].

228547721b672f7c0a272c87a5a67dec542eb178.answer:
The race distance is not a fixed number. Under Article B2.5.2, it is the least number of complete laps that exceeds 305 km [1].

There are two exceptions:
- **Monaco:** the race distance is the least number of complete laps that exceeds 260 km [1].
- **Safety Car start:** if the formation lap(s) is started behind the Safety Car, the number of race laps is reduced by the number of laps the Safety Car completes, minus one [1].

The passages do not give lap lengths, so they do not state the exact distance for any specific circuit. Passages [2] and [3] concern track running outside a competition and do not address race distance.

3ecc7b13d4511871e2198ad0acd95ebd95226b93.answer:
The passages don't give a single fixed race distance. The race distance is the least number of complete laps that exceeds 305km [1]. The race in Monaco is instead the least number of complete laps that exceeds 260km [1].

If the formation lap(s) start behind the Safety Car, the number of race laps is reduced by the number of Safety Car laps minus one [1].

The passages don't state the length of a lap, so they don't give the exact total distance.

f6c6a83358c604c745051a2c53baf51d72ac07d5.answer: Twelve (12) team members for each Competitor are permitted in the signalling area during any free practice session, qualifying session, sprint qualifying session, sprint session, and the Race [1].

0c02874be3e6b0864d73b24895d586b8b04694ce.answer: The provided passages do not cover how many mechanics can be on the grid before the start. They address topics such as cars moved from the grid to the Pit Lane before the formation lap [1], Power Unit element penalties [2], and race grid allocation and withdrawals [3], but none mention mechanics.

bd83092b7e740ed8a6e97f31471a1b600cf33200.answer: The provided passages do not specify how many mechanics can be on the grid before the start. f77c0c855d6320a9ac8d6ef2af70f3b5f6458090.answer: The passages don't use the term "jump start," but the false start rules in Article B5.11.1 appear to cover it. Under that article, cars must be stationary in their grid positions until the start signal, and the stewards can impose a **5-second penalty, a 10-second penalty, a drive-through penalty, or a stop-and-go penalty** on any driver judged to have breached this, at their sole discretion [3].

19531331ad2187b949f8792c64ec27051cc6dd55.answer:
The passages do not cover jump starts, so I can't say how one is penalised.

They do cover related situations. A Stop-and-Go Penalty is imposed on any driver who fails to start the TTCS from the Pit Lane [1][3]. Drivers who cause an aborted start and can then restart must start from the end of the Pit Lane [1]. Also, a Stop-and-Go Penalty imposed after a TTCS adds 30 seconds to the driver's elapsed time [2].

53b213b32b7faca1a5917f410bd5dc47395ce974.answer:
Yes, but only under conditions. Under Article B1.8.6, a driver who leaves the track may re-join, but only when it is safe to do so and without gaining any lasting advantage [1]. The Race Director may also, at their absolute discretion, give a driver the chance to give back the whole of any advantage gained by leaving the track [1].

The same article says drivers must make every reasonable effort to stay on the track and may not leave it without a justifiable reason [1].

786253151268182ed09008211919409ef0bb8a23.answer:
Yes, but only under conditions. A driver who leaves the track may re-join, but only when it is safe to do so and without gaining any lasting advantage [1]. At the Race Director's absolute discretion, a driver may be given the chance to give back the whole of any advantage gained by leaving the track [1].

Drivers are also expected to make every reasonable effort to stay on the track and may not leave it without a justifiable reason [1].

15be7d1f9332a81930d6785a371b97595ea5b7b0.answer: The provided passages do not cover how results are decided if a race is stopped and cannot be restarted. They describe the qualifying session timing [1], the procedure for an aborted start before the race begins [2], and the standing start resumption procedure after a Safety Car period [3], but none of them address a race that is halted permanently.

87bcfd760a425800a3dec5bcef0906cfc640a07e.answer:
The passages don't fully answer this. They only cover one consequence of a race that is suspended and cannot be restarted: the tyre-compliance penalty.

Under the tyre rules, if the race is suspended and cannot be re-started, 30 seconds is added to the elapsed time of any driver who did not, when required, use at least two specifications of dry-weather tyre during the race [1]. Disqualification applies only where the race is not suspended, or where it is suspended but can be restarted [1].

The passages do not explain how the final classification is otherwise determined in that situation. [2] covers resumption procedures for a Total Time Classified Session, and [3] covers interrupted Sprint Qualifying and Qualifying sessions, so neither addresses race results after a stoppage.

1950c360443e41d8c80a175c3933f03f02912707.answer: At a Standard Format Competition without additional tyres for ICTT, two sets of dry-weather tyres must be electronically returned no later than two hours after the end of FP1 [3].

05c150a9d13b3e6a352db13fa1371f1f9570dc16.answer: At a Standard Format Competition where additional tyres are not made available for ICTT, two sets of dry-weather tyres must be electronically returned no later than two hours after the end of FP1 [2].

66b95947180bb56962b03b2a935c30a2445356ae.answer:
Each driver gets **8 sets of soft-specification tyres** at a Standard Format Competition [1].

The table in [1] is garbled, but its first value column corresponds to the Standard Format Competition. If that competition includes ICTT (In-Competition Tyre Testing), the soft allocation drops to 6 sets [1][3].

9b84aa338599af19f85a90d90539b011d609404c.answer:
At a Standard Format Competition, each driver is allocated **8 sets of Soft Specification dry-weather tyres** [1].

The table also covers a Standard Format Competition with ICTT, where the allocation is 6 s

556c22a1be4c0698c824fd0a8ffbb94800b4c3a8.answer:
A driver must serve a 5-Second Penalty **the next time they enter the Pit Lane** [1]. There are two exceptions. The penalty is not served when entering the Pit Lane solely to follow the Safety Car, or when entering the Pit Lane after a red flag during a suspension procedure [1]. However, the driver must serve it if they choose to stop in their Designated Garage Area during a VSC or Safety Car procedure, including when following the Safety Car through the Pit Lane [1].

A driver may instead elect not to serve the penalty during the TTCS, provided they make no further pit stop before the TTCS ends. In that case, 5 seconds is added to their elapsed time [1][2]. If the penalty is imposed after the TTCS has ended, 5 seconds is added to the driver's elapsed time instead [3].

3d68adf1a9ff1a17fcc2402d56a0063ed7435ffa.answer:
A driver must serve a 5-Second Penalty **the next time they enter the Pit Lane** [1]. There are two exceptions: entering the Pit Lane solely to follow the Safety Car, or entering the Pit Lane following a red flag during a suspension procedure [1]. However, if the driver elects to stop in their Designated Garage Area while a VSC or Safety Car procedure is in use, including when following the Safety Car through the Pit Lane, they must serve the penalty [1].

The driver may instead elect not to serve the penalty during the TTCS, provided they make no further pit stop before the TTCS ends. In that case, 5 seconds is added to their elapsed time [1][2].

1a14b45f7732b44869b51bac26757a22c9e2579d.answer:
**Generally no, with a limited exception.** Work on a car in the Fast Lane is not allowed unless a specific exception applies.

- **General rule:** Competitors may not work on a car or leave equipment in the Fast Lane, except as specified in Articles B5.3.3 and B5.14.4a [3]. The Inner Lane is the only area for work on an F1 Car, except when F1 Cars are at the end of the Pit Lane under Articles B5.3 and B5.14 [2][3].

- **Exception (Article B5.3.3):** Work in the Fast Lane is permitted until 15 seconds before the formation lap begins. After that, all personnel and equipment must be clear. The permitted work is limited to:
  a. Starting the engine and directly associated preparation.
  b. Fitting or removing permitted cooling and heating devices.
  c. Changes made for driver comfort.
  d. Changing wheels and tyres, subject to Article B5.5.3.
  e. Adjusting the front wing profiles, where not controlled by the FIA Standard ECU, in accordance with Article C3.10.10. No parts may be added, removed, or replaced. [1]

  Drivers must follow marshals' directions at all times [1].

- **Additional restriction:** No work may be carried out in the Fast Lane if it is likely to hinder other F1 Cars trying to leave the Pit Lane [2][3].

3a31d9c210e321f47adf9ea308627a742fcf2dbd.answer:
The passages don't say whether a driver can receive physical help after stopping on the circuit during the Race and still rejoin.

The closest rules concern abandonment. Under [2], any F1 Car abandoned on the circuit by its driver, even temporarily, is considered withdrawn from the session, except during a TTCS suspension. Even then, a car may be allowed to rejoin only in exceptional circumstances and only if it was not abandoned because of a mechanical issue, car damage, or to gain an advantage. The passages do not say whether receiving physical help counts as abandonment or affects that status.

Under [3], a driver who abandons a car must leave it in neutral or with the clutch disengaged, with the ERS shut down and the steering wheel in place. The driver must also obey marshals' instructions and proceed without undue delay to a place of safety behind the barriers and debris fence.

742e1b35f1d05421f6cb492582e3832a106efd13.answer:
The passages do not directly answer this. None of them addresses receiving physical help after stopping on track during the Race.

They do cover related points:

- An F1 Car abandoned on the circuit by its driver, even temporarily, is considered withdrawn from the session, except during the suspension of a TTCS. In exceptional circumstances, a car abandoned during a TTCS suspension may take part when the session resumes, provided it was not abandoned because of a mechanical issue, car damage, or to gain an advantage [1].
- A driver who abandons a car must leave it in neutral or with the clutch disengaged, with the ERS shut down and the steering wheel in place. The driver must obey marshals' instructions and proceed without undue delay to a place of safety behind both lines of protection [2].

The weighing rules in [3] mention contact with other people only for drivers in the final period of Sprint Qualifying or Qualifying, so they do not apply to the Race.

598ae35131c00454f0b116f77a93a43dd574311f.answer:
Yes. Under Article B2.5.2, the Race distance is reduced when the formation lap(s) is started behind the Safety Car. In that case, the number of Race laps is reduced by the number of laps the Safety Car completes, minus one [1].

The same article also sets a different distance for the Monaco Grand Prix, which is the least number of complete laps exceeding 260km rather than 305km [1]. This is a shorter base distance, not a reduction triggered by a circumstance during the race.

2a1e2f7dbf62250c03140817fe5f475a45e92fbc.answer:
Yes. The Race distance is reduced when the formation lap(s) is started behind the Safety Car. In that case, the number of Race laps is reduced by the number of laps the Safety Car completes, minus one [1].

The Race distance is also set shorter at Monaco, at the least number of complete laps exceeding 260km rather than 305km [1]. This is a fixed, different distance for that event, not a reduction applied during a race.

68711be293313330a48c5d25429ab0857b76cb35.answer:
Generally, the passages suggest drivers cannot overtake while the Safety Car is deployed, but only the exceptions are spelled out. The passages do not state the general prohibition itself.

The exceptions include:

- **Pit areas:** While in the Pit Entry Road, Pit Lane or Pit Exit Road, a driver may overtake another F1 Car that is also in one of those areas, subject to Article B5.13.3 [2].
- **Stopped cars:** An F1 Car stopping in its Designated Garage Area while the Safety Car is using the Pit Lane may be overtaken [2].
- **Slow cars with an obvious problem:** Any F1 Car that slows with an obvious problem may be overtaken [2].
- **Cars required to pass:** When the Race Director instructs, the Safety Car's green light signals cars between it and the leader to pass. Once they have passed, the light goes out to signal that overtaking is no longer permitted, except in the cases listed in B5.13.2c [3].
- **Lapped cars:** If the Race Director considers it safe, the message "LAPPED CARS MAY NOW OVERTAKE" is sent, and lapped cars are required to pass the lead-lap cars and the Safety Car [3].

The Race Director can also block overtaking altogether. If track conditions are considered unsuitable, "OVERTAKING WILL NOT BE PERMITTED" is sent to all Competitors [3].

bf06363fb6be43cb511203da1c50b3bdb0f45d0e.answer:
No, not in general. When the Safety Car is deployed, Overtake is disabled [2]. It is re-enabled only after all F1 Cars have crossed the Control Line following the Safety Car's entry into the Pit Entry Road to return to the Pit Lane [2].

There are limited exceptions in the Safety Car provisions. While the Safety Car is deployed, a driver may overtake another F1 Car that is also in the Pit Entry Road, Pit Lane or Pit Exit Road, subject to Article B5.13.3 [1]. A car stopping in its Designated Garage Area while the Safety Car is using the Pit Lane may be overtaken [1]. A car that slows with an obvious problem may also be overtaken [1].

The excerpt begins at item vi, so items i to v of B5.13.2 are not included and may contain further exceptions.

5543da1ca0a3ad8b4402125f65124135bc29d3dc.answer:
A team can change parts on a car in parc fermé only in two situations:

1. **Work listed in Appendix B2.** The general rule is that no part of the car may be replaced or modified, but work listed in Appendix B2 is an exception [1].
2. **Work approved by the Technical Delegate under Article B3.5.4.** Parts may also be replaced with the Technical Delegate's approval [1]. Any parts replaced with the Technical Delegate's specific agreement while the cars are under parc fermé conditions must be published and distributed to all Competitors before the Race [2].

Outside these exceptions, no part may be replaced or modified, and no setup or configuration changes may be made [1]. Breaching this rule has consequences: the driver must start the Race from the Pit Lane at a Standard Format Competition, and at an Alternative Format Competition the start position depends on when the breach occurs [1].

d48d467f34d9c6c20bb5f4b76b9586d3b0e42617.answer:
A team may change parts on a car in parc fermé only in the limited cases below.

- **Work listed in Appendix B2 or approved by the Technical Delegate under Article B3.5.4.** Article B3.5.3 says no part may be replaced or modified, and no setup or configuration changed, except for this work [1]. Appendix B2 permits some work, including adjusting tyre pressures [3].

- **Survival cell replacement (Appendix B2, Article 11).** A car change is allowed if the original car suffered genuine accident damage or a significant failure or fault, and the survival cell must be changed. All components of the replacement car must match the original in design and be similar in mass, inertia, and function, and the suspension set-up must be the same [3].

- **Work requested by the Technical Delegate (Appendix B2, Article 12.2).** Any other work the Technical Delegate requests is permitted [3].

Other permitted items are a weighing using an allocated tyre set or travel tyres, and fitting exhaust extraction devices while starting the engine in the garage [3]. The Appendix also requires connecting the umbilical and starting telemetry logging for an ERS safety check immediately after covers are removed [3].

Changes that are not listed or approved are a breach. The penalty is a pit lane start: at a Standard Format Competition the driver starts the Race from the Pit Lane, and at an Alternative Format Competition

d4428eb9ef814d87b810ce635145772611e588c5.answer:
No, not necessarily. When a Heat Hazard is declared, all components of the Driver Cooling System must be fitted, except for the cooling medium and any items of the driver's personal equipment that form part of the system. At the start of a Sprint or Race, all components must be fitted and functional [2].

However, any driver may elect not to wear those personal equipment items. In that case, the other components, including the cooling medium, must still be fitted. The mass difference from the driver's normally used personal equipment must be compensated by 0.5kg of ballast in the cockpit [2]. That ballast may only be fitted after its mass is validated by the FIA Technical Delegate or their nominated representative, and under their direct supervision [1].

663c3266520d144109e3e136a88c600fc4d2d7f2.answer:
No, not necessarily. A driver must have the cooling system components fitted, but may choose not to wear the personal equipment parts of the system.

When a Heat Hazard is declared, all components of the Driver Cooling System must be fitted for the entire Competition, except the cooling medium and any personal equipment items that form part of the system [1]. At the start of any Sprint or Race covered by the declaration, all components must be fitted, functional, and available for the driver to use [1].

However, any driver may elect not to wear any items of personal equipment that form part of the system. In that case, all other components, including the cooling medium, must still be fitted. The driver must also add 0.5kg of ballast in the cockpit to compensate for the difference in mass between the personal equipment normally worn and the cooling equipment not worn [1]. That ballast must be validated by the FIA Technical Delegate or their representative and fitted under their direct supervision [2].

16be26a2e772c929a126acb4a58ea35508666859.answer:
Yes, but the car is disqualified rather than the driver. Under Article B3.2.3, the relevant F1 Car may be disqualified if it weighs less than the minimum specified in Article C4.1 when weighed under Articles B3.2.1 or B3.2.2 [1]. There is an exception: the car is not disqualified if the shortfall results from the accidental loss of a component [1].

Separately, Article B3.2.5 covers breaches of the weighing provisions. In that case, the stewards may drop the driver a number of grid positions they consider appropriate, or disqualify the driver from the TTCS [3]. The passages do not explicitly say whether an underweight car leads to driver disqualification under B3.2.5, so that question is not fully covered.

636a9e2c6ca3ef1e9bf7b84d89999813f4627814.answer: Possibly. The car, not the driver, is the subject of the rule. Under Article B3.2.3, the relevant F1 Car may be disqualified if it weighs less than the minimum specified in Article C4.1 when weighed under Article B3.2.1 or B3.2.2 [1]. The rule does not apply where the shortfall results from the accidental loss of a component of the car [1].

6f763705a28d7d89161dd3be12dda6f90288d26a.answer:
Yes, changes of driver are allowed after initial scrutineering, but only with the stewards' consent. Under Article B1.7.2, a change proposed after the end of initial scrutineering may be made if the stewards consent. The timing depends on the event:

- At a Competition without a scheduled sprint session, the change must be made before the start of the qualifying session [3].
- At a Competition with a scheduled sprint session, the change must be made before the start of the sprint qualifying session for a driver taking part in the sprint, or before the start of the qualifying session for a driver taking part in the Race [3].

Additional changes for force majeure are considered separately [3].

If a nominated driver is unable to drive after the end of initial scrutineering and the stewards consent to a change, the replacement driver must use the Power Unit and tyres allocated to the original driver [1].

e45e9a43baf78b36b4b4d1adfcea4bc7b584dd0e.answer:
Yes, but only with the stewards' consent. Under B1.7.2, any change proposed after the end of initial scrutineering must receive the stewards' consent [2]. Timing depends on the format:

- **Without a sprint session:** the change may be made at any time before the start of the qualifying session [2].
- **With a sprint session:** the change may be made before the start of the sprint qualifying session for a driver taking part in the sprint, or before the start of the qualifying session for a driver taking part in the Race [2].

Additional changes for reasons of force majeure are considered separately [2].

If a nominated driver becomes unable to drive after initial scrutineering and the stewards consent to a change, the replacement driver must use the Power Unit and tyres allocated to the original driver [1].

98d0f8afaa87cebfa82c62af1b82e964153283b4.answer: No. Refuelling is only permitted in the Competitors' designated garages [2]. The passages don't address refuelling in the pit lane outside the garage, so the answer rests on that rule.

1db1fba2c5e3d0cd2fdda57b040ccef36e0fe9fc.answer: No, refuelling is not allowed in the pit lane. Under Article B1.5.9(a), refuelling "is only permitted in the Competitors' designated garages" [3].

0002e4b39533d2c3a0b246ff1ba380f8e34c450e.answer: No. Article B1.6.1 states that competitors may not "use any powered device to lift any part of an F1 Car in the Pit Lane" [1].

85278596fbb7223f4aa53b608bbd8c0f6e6be343.answer: No. Under Article B1.6.1, competitors may not "use any powered device to lift any part of an F1 Car in the Pit Lane" [2].

ae7a8161e42722a06a9d81be406a7bc69ccafc3e.answer:
The passages don't give a direct answer for races. The only exception is during a suspension of a TTCS under Article B5.14, which is not included in the passages [1].

No, not while the car is being pushed. Once it is in the Pit Lane Inner Lane, the driver may try to start it. a451cabb79f6bcd370f0b03cae71c9ef211ad2c5.answer: No, not while it is being pushed from the grid. Under Article B5.7.1, "Any driver being pushed from the grid may not attempt to start the F1 Car" [1]. If the start is successful, the car may enter the Fast Lane only after the TTCS has started, and it may then join the TTCS [1].

The document does not cover whether a team can cover its car in the pit lane when it rains.

f7c99f4261da779497315903e9736ab80f015781.answer:
The passages don't give a definitive answer. Drive-Through Penalties are named in [3], which sets out how they are served, but none of the passages says which article governs them.

[2] states that appeals may not be made against penalties imposed under Articles B1.9.5 a. to h. The passages don't directly confirm that a Race is covered. The penalty list in [2] applies to "any TTCS," and the passages don't define TTCS or state that a Race is one. Assuming it applies, for an incident during a TTCS the stewards may impose any one of these penalties on any driver involved:

- A 5-second time penalty, served by entering the Pit Lane and stopping in the Designated Pit Stop Position for at least five seconds [2].
- A 10-second time penalty, served the same way but for at least ten seconds [2].
- A drive-through penalty, served by entering the Pit Lane and rejoining without stopping [2].
- A 10-second stop-and-go penalty, served by stopping in the Designated Pit Stop Position for at least ten seconds [2].
- A time penalty [2].
- A driver reprimand [2].
- A Competitor (F1 Team) reprimand [2].

A driver who receives five reprimands, at least four for driving infringements, in the same Championship receives a 10-grid-place penalty. If the fifth reprimand follows an incident during a Race, that penalty applies at the driver's next Competition [2].

Stewards have discretion over whether to penalise a driver involved in an incident.

acc67a78b3402a1319e51172fce7fbb152ca0ac2.answer:

6078bccea726d50c18b629122d4fd5cd38753616.answer: Drivers with more than 15 cumulative grid penalties for the Race start behind any other classified driver. Their relative order among themselves is set by their Qualifying classification [2].

c44f16391019dc632b3fd9d9ea36d1335d610cfb.answer: Drivers with more than 15 cumulative grid position penalties for the Race start behind any other classified driver. Their relative position among themselves is determined by their Qualifying classification [1].

14b374c76a4e45433a782fd8910390905d98fb03.answer: Three sets of dry-weather tyres must be electronically returned no later than the covers-on time after Qualifying, as defined in Article B3.4.3 [1]. The passages do not state the exact clock time, so the definition in Article B3.4.3 would be needed for that.

79a6e94f3245d79719ce030f70dbe9e9f4081b81.answer:
Three sets of dry-weather tyres must be electronically returned no later than the covers-on time after Qualifying, as defined in Article B3.4.3 [1]. This applies during an Alternative Format Competition, which includes Sprint weekends [1].

The passages do not give the actual time. Article B3.4.3, which defines the covers-on time, is not included.

072082cfd4ef7ffb0c305e721a23050d2a45ce6a.answer: The provided passages do not cover prize money. They address the circulation of instructions and results [1], a limit on track running mileage for testing [2], and podium ceremony obligations for the top three finishers [3]. None of them state what the Race winner receives.

a7490ffaab1a24444ad15d805d527d39f654e74c.answer: The provided passages do not cover how much prize money the Race winner receives. They describe the podium ceremony obligations for the top three drivers and a constructor representative [1], driver change limits [2], and track running mileage limits [3], but none of them mention prize money.

777e697fec8471ba2769d595015c2cea9e01e57c.answer:
The passages don't give an exact minimum. Under the general rule, a Sprint's distance is the least number of complete laps that exceeds 100 km [1]. The exact figure would therefore depend on the circuit's lap length, which the passages don't provide.

The rule has an exception: if the formation lap is started behind the Safety Car, the number of Sprint laps is reduced by the number of Safety Car laps minus one [1]. The passages don't state how far this could take the distance below 100 km.

7fe4bdb5c503c5ddd954d6f7decd1e51224e5d08.answer:
The passages set the Sprint distance as the least number of complete laps that exceeds 100km [1]. So the distance is always just over 100km, but the exact minimum depends on the circuit's lap length, which the passages don't give. The document does not state a fixed minimum in kilometres.

One exception applies: if the formation lap(s) start behind the Safety Car, the number of Sprint laps is reduced by the Safety Car's laps minus one [1]. That reduction could take the distance below 100km, though the passages don't say so explicitly.

c11db678adc8290c944c84cec4fda15e9e7aad05.answer:
A Sprint's time limit is **one hour from the start signal**. At that point the leader is shown the end-of-session signal when they cross the Control Line at the end of the lap following the lap during which the hour ended, provided this does not exceed the scheduled number of laps [1].

If the Sprint is suspended, the length of the suspension is added to the one-hour period, up to a **maximum total Sprint duration of one and a half (1.5) hours**. The same end-of-lap rule and laps-limit proviso apply [1].

The scheduled distance is the least number of complete laps exceeding 100km, so a Sprint may also end when that distance is completed [3].

3a307dcd521c4cca476bf35a0497b6514dec9363.answer:
A Sprint is normally limited to **one hour** from the start signal. Once that hour elapses, the leader is shown the end-of-session signal when they cross the Control Line at the end of the lap following the lap during which the hour ended, provided this does not exceed the scheduled number of laps [1].

If the Sprint is suspended, the suspension time is added to the one-hour period, up to a **maximum total Sprint duration of one and a half (1.5) hours**. The same rule applies: the leader is shown the signal at the end of the lap following the one during which the combined period ended, again without exceeding the scheduled laps [1].

The chequered flag is the end-of-session signal, and it is subject to these Sprint exceptions [3].

a274598040b644312cd492c46ff32ca7dc3f8b27.answer:
If Sprint Qualifying does not take place and the Stewards accept that it cannot, the Sprint grid is based on the Drivers' Championship classification. The grid is set using the same steps as the normal procedure, but each driver's Drivers' Championship classification replaces their Sprint Qualifying classification, and all drivers are treated as classified [1].

If neither method can be applied, the Stewards decide the grid at their sole discretion [1].

697736a5b3af16f24589aa6cbfe8ecb5d79aaa2b.answer: The first period of Sprint Qualifying, SQ1, lasts twelve minutes. During that time all F1 Cars may take to the track, and at the end the slowest six are eliminated [2].

0363f8a0a7affb3a326f75b0405471de75480907.answer: The first period of Sprint Qualifying (SQ1) lasts twelve minutes. All F1 Cars may take to the track during this period, and at its end the slowest six are eliminated [1].

94289a0c048577d9741cc924ac860e621776b8c9.answer: The second period of Qualifying is Qualifying 2 (Q2), which lasts fifteen minutes. After a seven-minute break, the sixteen remaining F1 Cars take to the track, and the slowest six are then eliminated [2].

88ef48cc62f235da6dea65eaf0434b27b72577f4.answer: The second period of Qualifying is Qualifying 2 (Q2), which runs for fifteen minutes. It begins after a seven-minute break following Q1 [2].

09704744eb12ba19afe49659d44842919ede63ec.answer:
The message is **"SAFETY CAR IN THIS LAP."** It is sent to all Competitors when the Race Director decides it is safe to end the Safety Car period, and the Safety Car's orange lights are extinguished at the same time. This signals that the Safety Car will enter the Pit Lane at the end of that lap [1].

Under a rolling start, the message "ROLLING START" is sent instead, and it also signals that the Safety Car will enter the Pit Lane at the end of that lap [3]. The passages describe this as a formation-lap procedure rather than the end of a Safety Car period.

2447f09a460ba18300bbc5a6f025555f0254309f.answer: The Virtual Safety Car is used when double waved yellow flags are needed on any section of track and competitors or officials may be in danger, but the circumstances do not warrant the Safety Car [1]. By contrast, the Safety Car is used only if competitors or officials are in immediate physical danger on or near the track, but the circumstances do not require suspending the session [2]. The passages describe these thresholds separately and do not explicitly say the VSC replaces the SC, so the distinction rests on the difference in the danger level described.

51d5ec80798d477f9b580382cc65e700bf87c94a.answer: The Virtual Safety Car is used when double waved yellow flags are needed on any section of track and competitors or officials may be in danger, but the circumstances are not serious enough to warrant the Safety Car [1].

7ee6ca2b0b525d913b7d866a78a9ab6e0394951f.answer:
Cars queued behind the Safety Car may be separated by no more than **ten (10) car lengths**. All F1 Cars must form up in a queue behind the Safety Car with that maximum gap [1].

In poor visibility, the Race Director may, at their sole discretion, increase the maximum gap to **twenty (20) car lengths**. This applies between F1 Cars, including between the first car and the Safety Car, and is announced with the message "LOW VISIBILITY – MAXIMUM GAP TWENTY CAR LENGTHS" [1][2]. The same ten-car-length rule and poor-visibility increase apply to the grid-order formation lap behind the Safety Car [3].

8490f9fbe8a87617d5838b1aefcb69e12644ad16.answer:
Under normal conditions, the cars queued behind the Safety Car may be no more than **ten (10) car lengths** apart. Article B5.13.2 requires all F1 Cars to "form up in a queue behind the Safety Car no more than the maximum allowable gap of ten (10) car lengths apart" [2]. The same ten-car-length limit applies on the formation lap [1] and during the resumption procedure [3].

In poor visibility, the Race Director may, at their sole discretion, increase the maximum allowable gap to **twenty (20) car lengths**. The Race Director must then send the message "LOW VISIBILITY – MAXIMUM GAP TWENTY CAR LENGTHS" to all Competitors [2][3].

10d6dfdc131fb981df23d21fa476c9474438aa4f.answer:
The passages don't directly answer this. They do not mention free practice or list the sessions where the VSC may be used.

The rule is in Article B5, under Total Time Classified Sessions (TTCS). It applies when double waved yellow flags are needed on a section of track, and competitors or officials may be in danger, but the circumstances don't warrant a Safety Car [1].

Some provisions are worded as applying only "when initiated during a TTCS," such as the pit lane restriction and the stewards' penalty powers [2][3]. This implies the VSC can also be initiated outside a TTCS, but the passages don't say so explicitly or name the sessions where that applies.

a9d2001f54a9914e798f7970d3266d4ed1bc97d0.answer:
The passages don't address qualifying specifically, but they set out the stewards' general powers over any incident, which would apply there:

- **Decide whether to investigate:** The stewards decide whether to proceed with an investigation. They may also investigate an incident they notice themselves [3]. The Race Director may report incidents or suspected breaches to them [2].
- **Notify competitors:** If an incident is under investigation, a message naming the drivers involved is sent to all competitors [3].
- **Restrict drivers' movements:** Provided that message is displayed no later than 60 minutes after the end-of-session signal of a TTCS, the drivers concerned may not leave the circuit without the stewards' consent [3].
- **Decide on penalties:** The stewards decide whether a driver involved in an incident should be penalised. No penalty is imposed unless it is clear that the driver was wholly or predominantly to blame [1].
- **Choose the penalty:** They may impose penalties specifically set out in the FIA F1 Regulations, either in addition to or instead of other penalties available under the ISC [1].

d26e1e606586aa269f9ef7fb9042de60f49e06d4.answer:
During a Lap Time Competition Session (LTCS), the stewards may:

- **Delete a driver's lap time or lap times**, or
- **Drop the driver a number of grid positions** that they consider appropriate [1].

Incidents are normally investigated after the relevant session, unless it is completely clear that a driver committed a driving infringement [1]. Stewards also decide whether to investigate an incident at all, and they may investigate incidents they noticed themselves [2].

Grid position penalties are served in the Race. The exception is an infringement during Sprint Qualifying, where the penalty is applied to the Sprint grid [1].

When deciding whether to penalise a driver involved in an incident, stewards have discretion. No penalty is imposed unless the driver is clearly wholly or predominantly to blame. Stewards may impose penalties set out in the regulations either in addition to or instead of other available penalties [3].

The passages do not explicitly state that Qualifying is an LTCS, so this answer assumes it is.

17b35760fc61843179f85de4de22429acf75dbfb.answer: A grid position penalty for an incident during Sprint Qualifying is served on the grid of the Sprint. Under Article B1.9.4(b), penalties for incidents during a LTCS are normally served in the Race, but "unless the driving infringement occurred in the Sprint Qualifying, in which case such penalty will be applied to the grid of the Sprint" [2].

e1d93e05c2305c26952ed6db184bc58dff2502f1.answer:
A grid position penalty for an incident in Sprint Qualifying is applied to the grid of the Sprint, not the Race. Normally, such penalties are served in the Race, but if the driving infringement occurred in Sprint Qualifying, the penalty goes to the Sprint grid [1].

This is consistent with the Sprint grid rules, which add up any penalties received for the Sprint and apply them when forming the Sprint grid [3].

4b17ab88942c2dbc44f0e3fba554f87e151a0989.answer: There is one free practice session at each Alternative Format Competition: "Free Practice 1" (FP1), lasting one hour, on the first day of on-track running [1].

9be0ad5c141762225c56238ed61c19716d33186d.answer: The second free practice session (FP2) lasts **one and a half (1.5) hours** when additional tyre specifications are provided for ICTT. Otherwise, FP2 is one hour. [1]

792adbbd6f92bb75ef6e27ad58d2db0dd422cd9e.answer: The second free practice session (FP2) lasts **one and a half (1.5) hours** when additional tyre specifications are provided for ICTT. Normally it lasts one hour. [1]

9b4722e26a9aef5e743eaadf48d2d4f612fd61e8.answer: A driver must return one set of dry-weather tyres no later than two hours after the end of the Sprint. If the driver used a set during the Sprint, that returned set must be the one with the highest number of laps completed in the Sprint [2].

6c3840bbef6eca4fa800acc010bffc8089524fc2.answer:
A driver must return one set of dry-weather tyres within two hours after the end of the Sprint [1]. If the driver used a set during the Sprint, the returned set must be the one with the highest number of laps completed in the Sprint [1].

The passages do not describe any intermediate or wet-weather tyre that must be returned within two hours of the Sprint ending.

ed1a639c2218c922d59c009dac27babf64af7157.answer:
The passages do not directly answer this. None of them covers a car that breaks down on its way to the grid.

The closest rules concern cars that are already on the grid. Under B5.7.2, cars starting from the grid must return to the grid at the end of the formation lap and stop within their starting grid positions [3]. Under B5.11.1, during a standing start all cars must be stationary in their allocated grid position when the start signal is given [2].

Article B5.5.6 deals with a different case. A car that has stopped on the grid and is then moved to the Pit Lane Inner Lane or the Competitors Designated Garage Area before the formation lap cannot return to the grid before the TTCS starts. If it is able to, it must start from the Pit Lane [1].

10838bf2826b77e671659091fc2c9886f82fabc9.answer:
Overtaking behind the Safety Car is allowed in two situations, and in both the green light on the Safety Car is the signal that governs it.

**1. Cars between the Safety Car and the leader.** When the Race Director instructs, the green light on the Safety Car is illuminated, and F1 Cars between it and the leader are required to pass it. [3] Once all of those cars have passed, the green light is extinguished, and overtaking is no longer permitted. [3] The cars that have passed then continue at reduced speed, without overtaking, until they reach the queue behind the Safety Car. [3]

**2. Lapped cars.** If the Race Director considers it safe, the message "LAPPED CARS MAY NOW OVERTAKE" is sent, and the green light illuminates to tell lapped F1 Cars that they must pass the lead-lap cars and the Safety Car. [3] This applies only to cars that were lapped when they crossed the Control Line at the end of the lap on which they first crossed the Saf

103246894ce372037612a503623b85d083c01adf.answer: **Overtaking during the formation lap(s):** Overtaking is allowed only in limited cases, including when a car is delayed leaving the grid and cars behind cannot avoid it without unduly delaying the field, when a car slows with an obvious problem, or when a car is delayed during the formation lap [1]. Even then, drivers may overtake only to restore the original starting order or the order at the Pit Lane exit when the formation lap started [1]. In a standing start, a delayed driver may overtake to regain the original starting position only before crossing the first safety car line on the lap the Safety Car returns to the pits. If they f

6df099b89ad4f4d68c591fa984d545c53fb6357b.answer:
The passages don't describe a "halted start" as such, but they cover the two procedures that follow the formation laps, standing and rolling starts. Under those procedures:

**Where the cars go:**
- **Standing start:** Once the Safety Car has entered the Pit Lane, all F1 Cars except those required to start from the Pit Lane can return to the grid and take their grid positions. Cars required to start from the Pit Lane must re-enter the Pit Lane and may start once the Pit Lane exit opens after the start. [2]
- **Rolling start:** Drivers keep moving at a steady pace until the Safety Car enters the Pit Entry Road, with no erratic acceleration or braking and no car driven alongside another car ahead. [3]

**Order:**

aa6ba75aa64ef71fbfc742cf83dd00297862b100.answer:
If the start is suspended after the formation laps behind the Safety Car have begun, all F1 Cars must enter the Pit Lane behind the Safety Car [1].

- **First car:** It should go directly to the Pit Lane exit, unless the Race Director has defined a different location in the Pit Lane [1].
- **Other cars:** They form up in a line behind the first car, in the order they entered the Pit Lane behind the Safety Car when the start was suspended. All cars must stay in the Fast Lane [1].

In exceptional circumstances, if the pit entry is closed for safety reasons before all F1 Cars have returned, the cars must proceed slowly to the starting grid instead. The first car to arrive on the grid takes pole position, and the others fill the remaining positions in the order they arrive [1]. In either case, the procedures in Article B5.15 must then be followed [1].

a179a740f5d065f06bcc6e698d7b022317d1998f.answer:
The provided passages do not answer this. None of them states how many people working on the cars a team may have at the circuit during a race weekend, or whether that limit applies on race day.

The closest passage is Article B9.5.3 [3]. It gives each Competitor a number of exceptions to the Article B9.5 requirements during the Championship: six for Restricted Period One, five for Restricted Period Two, and four for Restricted Period Three. It also says these exceptions may not be used consecutively during a single Competition. However, it does not define the Article B9.5 requirements themselves, so it cannot tell you the headcount limit. For a breach, both drivers must start the Race from the Pit Lane under Article B5.3.

Article B1.7.1 [2] limits each Competitor to four drivers in Races during a Championship, but it concerns drivers, not personnel.

To find the headcount rule and whether it applies on race day, you would need Article B9.5 itself, which is not included here.

87754c316901c020d6f90c12ab9dd03e20625ae6.answer:
A team may have at most **60 Operational Personnel** at the circuit, meaning people associated in any way with operating the F1 Cars within the circuit. This applies from 29 hours before the scheduled start of FP1 until 2 hours after the start of the Race [1].

**On race day, the limit still applies only in part.** It is lifted from 45 minutes before the start of the first formation lap until 15 minutes after the scheduled start of the Race, when the number of Operational Personnel is unlimited [1]. Before that window opens, the 60-person cap still applies.

A separate restriction covers the signalling area. Only twelve team members per Competitor are permitted there during free practice, qualifying, sprint qualifying, sprint, and the Race [2]. This is a limit on the signalling area specifically, not on total personnel at the circuit, and the passages do not say whether it is affected by the unlimited window.

7b0a985f1f362a486d4cd61a437adcc3fe4605bb.answer:
The passages don't give a fixed delay for the Safety Car. Under Article B5.13.6, when the Race Director decides to end the Safety Car period, the "SAFETY CAR IN THIS LAP" message is sent and the Safety Car's orange lights are extinguished. The green flag and/or green light panel is shown at the Control Line as the leader approaches it, and this happens on the final lap, not after a set number of seconds [2].

The 10 to 15 second delay before green lights and the 30 second switch-off apply to the Virtual Safety Car, not the Safety Car. For the VSC, the "VSC" lights turn green between 10 and 15 seconds after the "VSC ENDING" message, and go out 30 seconds after that [1].

bb497eb4b53f3284a189aea13fe3a22167288667.answer:
The passages don't give this timing for the Safety Car. For the Safety Car, the Race Director's decision triggers the message "SAFETY CAR IN THIS LAP," and the orange lights on the Safety Car are extinguished. That passage doesn't mention green lights or a timing for them [2].

The 10-15 second and 30-second timings apply to the Virtual Safety Car. After the Race Director decides to end the VSC procedure and sends "VSC ENDING," the "VSC" light on the FIA light panels can turn green at any time between 10 and 15 seconds later. After 30 seconds, the green lights are extinguished [1][3].

a6f17abc549c9a4192e8ea1a367eda0d1f001280.answer:
The passages do not cover this. None of them address qualifying being cancelled or stewards deciding a session cannot run.

The closest related rule is the aborted start procedure. If the Race Director aborts a start after the formation lap has begun, cars starting from the grid stay in their allocated grid positions, and cars starting from the Pit Lane stay in their position in the Fast Lane [1]. When a new start time is known, the starting procedure restarts at the ten-minute signal [1]. This applies to an aborted start, not to a cancelled session, so it may not apply to your situation.

9c6ec4a9ab03fac3107c6baec619e458519eb097.answer:
The passages do not say what happens to the starting order if qualifying is cancelled and the stewards agree it cannot run.

They do cover related points:

- Race Director authority: The Race Director has overriding authority over stopping qualifying "if they deem it unsafe to continue," and may propose timetable changes to the stewards [3]. The passages do not say what grid results from a stopped or cancelled session.
- Ordering of unclassified drivers: Drivers who are unclassified in the Race Qualifying classification because they were eliminated in Q1 beyond 107% (unless the track was declared wet), or who set no valid lap, are ordered by their position in the last LTCS in which all such drivers took part [1]. Drivers disqualified from qualifying are placed behind them [1]. This applies to unclassified drivers within a running session, not to a cancelled one.
- Formation lap: Article B5.6.4 covers overtaking to re-establish the starting order on the formation lap, not how that order is set when qualifying does not run [2].

65df7096aa3f28adfe0bb9c4a9ca7a270e894d2b.answer:
The provided passages do not say who, besides drivers, is allowed on the track or in the pit lane during practice, qualifying, or sprint sessions.

Passage [1] says that pit lane and track discipline and safety measures are the same for free practice, qualifying, sprint qualifying, sprint, and the Race, unless the regulations say otherwise. It does not list the permitted personnel. Passage [3] limits use of the circuit for non-competition purposes to times after the final practice session of each day, after Sprint Qualifying and Qualifying, and on race day before the Pit Lane exit opens. It also does not name who may be present during sessions. Passage [2] concerns drivers whose cars stop and receive physical assistance, but it does not address other people.

8566967b04f8e820d1847cad5680804e851d04e8.answer:
Besides drivers, the following are allowed on the track, the Pit Entry Road, or the Pit Exit Road during the period from 15 minutes before to 5 minutes after each free practice, qualifying, and sprint qualifying session [2]:

- **Marshals or other authorised personnel**, when carrying out their duties [2].
- **F1 Team personnel**, when pushing an F1 Car, or when clearing equipment from the grid after all F1 Cars able to leave have left the grid on the formation lap [2].
- **F1 Team personnel**, when assisting marshals to remove an F1 Car from the grid after the start of the TTCS [2].

9ae2b2b919df4b5e6b40fb0e8c943f6dfa6161fa.answer:
The passages don't mention Q1 or Q2 by name, but they do explain how the race grid is set from Qualifying results. Drivers knocked out in Q1 or Q2 would be placed according to their overall Qualifying classification, the same way as every other classified driver.

- **Starting point:** The race grid is formed from the Qualifying results and classification process, and any race penalties are then applied [2].
- **Penalised drivers (15 or fewer grid penalties):** Each gets a temporary position equal to their Qualifying classification plus their grid penalties. Ties are resolved by Qualifying classification [2].
- **Unpenalised classified drivers:** They fill any remaining open positions in Qualifying order [2][1].
- **Penalised drivers with temporary positions:** They move up to fill any gaps left after unpenalised drivers are placed [1].
- **Drivers with more than 15 cumulative grid penalties:** They start behind all other classified drivers, ordered by Qualifying classification [1].
- **Unclassified drivers allowed to take part by the Stewards:** They start behind all classified drivers [1].

6700539670934e21beddb9050954ba6b46d1ef81.answer:
Drivers eliminated in Q1 and Q2 are placed by their fastest lap time in the session where they were knocked out:

- **Eliminated in Q2 (positions 11–16):** These drivers are ordered by their fastest Q2 lap time, with the fastest in 11th place. [2]
- **Eliminated in Q1 (positions 17–22):** These drivers are ordered by their fastest Q1 lap time, with the fastest in 17th place. [2]

Some tie-break and edge rules also apply:

- **Identical times:** The driver who set the time first gets the higher position. [2]
- **Multiple drivers with no time in Q2:** Drivers who attempted a flying lap rank ahead of those who did not start one, and those who never left the pits rank last. Within each group, the order follows their previous session classification. [2]
- **Unclassified drivers:** Drivers who were eliminated in Q1 with a best lap over 107% of the fastest Q1 time (unless the track was declared wet), or who set no valid lap, or who were disqualified from qualifying, are placed unclassified. Those unclassified for the first two reasons are placed by their last fully participated session's order, and those disqualified are placed behind them. [1]
- **Valid laps only:** Only laps started and completed by crossing the Control Line on the track count. [1][3]

The number of drivers eliminated depends on the field size. The procedures assume 22 cars, and

c2776d3ea31f1dcb73e78ed350dd57dc947683cc.answer:
The provided passages do not cover this. None of them address stop-and-go penalties, stalled engines, or whether mechanics may help restart a car in the pit lane.

The closest material is limited:

- Article B5.7.3 covers the pit lane start procedure, where cars must keep their engines running while queuing at the pit lane exit [1]. It does not address restarting a stalled engine.
- Article B5.13.3 covers pit lane use during a Safety Car deployment and a drive-through penalty for failing to enter the pit lane when required [2]. It does not mention stop-and-go penalties or stalls.
- Appendix B2 lists permitted parc fermé works, such as safety checks, fluid work, and repairs [3]. It does not mention restarting an engine, and the passages don't establish whether a car serving a penalty is in parc fermé.

For an answer on this scenario, check the full regulations or ask the race stewards or FIA officials.

ecc2c26685dd1a25ac14419cb18ff9c05869e69f.answer: No. If the engine stops and you cannot restart it unaided, any work needed to restart it may only be carried out after the time penalty period has elapsed [1]. While the car is stationary in the Pit Lane for a Stop-and-Go Penalty, it may not be worked on, and touching the car or driver by hand, with tools, or with other equipment all count as working [1].

5ec2c7cf3b9b78d02a1facd5677752caa65a2a95.answer:
The provided passages do not cover this. They don't address parc fermé, when a car is locked away after leaving the pit lane in qualifying, or what happens if a car never leaves the pit lane.

The passages do cover some related topics:

- **Circuit use:** Unless the FIA gives written permission, the circuit may be used for non-competition purposes only after the last free practice session each day, after Sprint Qualifying, after Qualifying, and on race day at least one hour before the Pit Lane exit opens for reconnaissance laps [1].
- **Pit lane layout:** The Pit Entry Road runs from the first safety car line to the start of the Pit Lane, and the Pit Exit Road runs from the end of the Pit Lane to the second safety car line [2].
- **Restricted Period:** This is defined as a period when team personnel associated with operating the F1 Cars are not permitted within the circuit confines, but the passage does not say when it applies [2].
- **Safety car pit lane use:** If the Race Director orders the pit lane to be used during a safety car deployment, a drive-through penalty applies to any driver who fails to enter it [3]. This applies only to safety car situations, not to qualifying.

For the parc fermé rules you're asking about, you'd need the section of the regulations that covers parc fermé and qualifying.

416c83f73eda5b6302735e8c5c8ec1444bacb17e.answer:
Once your car first leaves the pit lane during qualifying, it is deemed to be in parc fermé from that moment until the start of the Race [1].

If it never leaves the pit lane during qualifying, it is deemed to be in parc fermé at the end of Q1 [1].

70f68f5806a62a2ad1cc2050a3f004ec55d56be0.answer:
The passages don't directly say which older parts a team may use in pre-season testing. The pre-season tests in [3] (the Private Collective Testing and the two Public Collective Testing sessions) set out running days and car limits but say nothing about component age.

The closest rules concern the **Post-Season Test**, which takes place after the last race of the championship and so falls before the next season's first race:

- The car for tyre testing "must only use components and software of a specification that have been used in at least one (1) Race or TCC during the current year or the year preceding the year of the Champion

94a93d0fe28c7a79d60ff055dd612daf4e61705a.answer:
The provided passages don't cover testing before the first race of the season. The closest rule, Article B11.4.10c, applies only to tests run between the end of the first Competition and 31 December [1]. It lets a team use Mule Cars that meet one of two conditions:

- **Option i:** a car built to the current Championship's technical regulations, using only components and software that were used in at least one Race or TCC in the current year or the four years before it [1].
- **Option ii:** a car built to the technical regulations of any of the four calendar years before the Championship year, using only components and software that were used in at least one Race or TCC in those four years [1].

The other passages cover the Post-Season Test, which takes place after the last Competition of the season. Its F1 Cars may only use components used in a Race or TCC in the current year or the preceding year [2]. The Out-of-Competition Tyre Testing and TPC rules in [3] restrict test parts and component changes, but they don't set out which older parts may be used before the first race.

0e97ff0d5313573a54c527c245f7d4a6e9b37cb9.answer:
Your mechanics must wait until the penalty's time period has elapsed. Under the stop-and-go rules, an F1 Car stationary in the Pit Lane for a Stop-and-Go Penalty may not be worked on. Touching the car or driver by hand or with tools counts as working. If the engine stops and the driver cannot restart it unaided, any work needed to restart it may only be carried out after the time penalty period has elapsed [1].

The passage does not state the length of that period, so I can't give you a specific number of seconds.

c519d315b880a1fd1a36d5320d944393aa65d9fd.answer:
Under the rules, your mechanics may not work on the car until the penalty's time period has elapsed, but only if the engine stops and the driver cannot restart it unaided. Touching the car or driver by hand, with tools, or with other equipment all count as working. [2]

The passages do not state the length of the time penalty period for a stop-and-go penalty in the pit lane. They give fixed time additions for other situations, such as when a penalty is served after a TTCS ends or during the last three laps, but those are added to the driver's elapsed time, not used as the waiting period. [1][2]

fb51be6978b7e7b1ff4b908e0523985a59883b6e.answer:
The passages cover one tyre-related running window, the Post-Season Test, and some related items, but not a complete set of tyre-check rules.

**Post-Season Test (tyre specifications for the following season):**
- **When:** One test, one day long. It must start no less than 36 hours after the end of the last Competition of the Championship [2].
- **Where:** On the circuit where the last Competition of the Championship was held [2].
- **Car use:** One of the two F1 Cars each Competitor must run is for providing Competitors with the chance to test the tyre specifications to be used the following season. That car must use components and software that have been used in at least one Race or TCC in the current year or the preceding year, though this does not apply to Power Units or their associated software [2].
- **Sensors:** Additional sensors may be fitted only to measure tyre state or performance. They must be agreed in advance with the Tyre Supplier and the FIA, and the data must be shared with the Tyre Supplier [3].

**Wet-weather tyre testing:** One day may be set aside if the Tyre Supplier requests it. Arrangements are made in consultation with all Competitors, the Commercial Rights Holder and the FIA [2]. The passage gives no time or location limits for this day.

**Out-of-Competition Tyre Testing

02c00767fc64e7369c7dec0d2d2640abeeee758a.answer:
The provided passages don't fully answer this. They don't set out when Out-of-Competition Tyre Testing may take place, and they don't give any time or location limits for it. The full text of Article B11.2.7d, which defines that testing, isn't included.

Here is what the passages do say:

- **Permitted cars:** For Out-of-Competition Tyre Testing, the car on track must be a Current Car, a Previous Car, or a Mule Car. Any other type of automobile is not allowed [2].
- **Set-up changes:** Mechanical set-up and driver control changes are allowed only if they are necessary to evaluate the tyres or complete the tyre test. These changes must be agreed in advance with the tyre supplier [3].

The passages also describe a different type of running, Testing for TMC (B11.4.10). That testing is limited to a maximum of ten car days between 1 January and 31 December, organised by the FIA. It also has circuit-related conditions for testing before a Competition [1]. These limits apply to TMC testing and should not be assumed to apply to tyre testing. If you need the timing and location rules for tyre checks, you'll need Article B11.2.7d or the relevant section of the regulations.

27006111241932998246d552dda0c0ca74cc452c.answer:
Under the resumption rules, drivers may overtake during a rolling start only to re-establish the resumption order, and only before the message "ROLLING START" is sent to all competitors [1]. This applies only in the permitted cases: a Fast Lane car leaving its position with an obvious problem, a Pit Lane overtake, a car slowing with an obvious problem, or a car delayed during the lap(s) behind the Safety Car [1].

If a driver does not re-establish the order before that message, they must resume the TTCS from where they are [1]. The formation-lap rules use the same cutoff for a rolling start [2].

c57bfca5481a0298457d9850aae22e007d311527.answer:
Under a rolling start, drivers may not overtake again until they pass the Control Line for the first time after the Safety Car has entered the Pit Entry Road to return to the Pit Lane [1][3]. The TTCS starts when the leading car crosses that line [1][3].

Until then, drivers must keep a pace with no erratic acceleration or braking, and no part of an F1 car may be driven alongside any part of a car ahead [3].

9fbb10e0310a3547ef2c3fd30a664c0394d6f720.answer:
Normally, cars queued behind the Safety Car must stay no more than ten car lengths apart, and the first car must stay less than ten car lengths behind the Safety Car [2].

Yes, the limit changes in poor visibility. At the sole discretion of the Race Director, the maximum gap between F1 cars, including between the first car and the Safety Car, can increase to twenty car lengths. When this happens, the message "LOW VISIBILITY – MAXIMUM GAP TWENTY CAR LENGTHS" is sent to all competitors [2][3].

6ca3e4da060dc54a0535cdc50c933051e9966641.answer:
Normally, cars queued behind the Safety Car must be no more than **ten car lengths apart**. Article B5.13.2 requires all F1 Cars to "form up in a queue behind the Safety Car no more than the maximum allowable gap of ten (10) car lengths apart" [2].

**Yes, the limit changes in poor visibility.** At the sole discretion of the Race Director, the maximum gap between F1 Cars, including between the first car and the Safety Car, may be increased to **twenty car lengths**. Competitors are notified with the message "LOW VISIBILITY – MAXIMUM GAP TWENTY CAR LENGTHS" [2]. The same provision applies during the resumption procedure [3] and the formation lap [1].

1e60d2968eaff875ccb1f84688b3fc31add6e6bc.answer:
Generally, no. A driver with a Drive-Through or Stop-and-Go Penalty may not serve it while the Virtual Safety Car procedure is in use or after the Safety Car has been deployed, with one exception: if the driver was already in the Pit Entry Road or Pit Lane for the purpose of serving the penalty [1]. Any Control Line crossings made behind the Safety Car or during the VSC are added to the driver's maximum allowed crossings [1].

The passage does not explicitly name the two penalty types in that clause, but the following clause refers to "either of these two (2) penalties," which indicates that it covers Drive-Through and Stop-and-Go Penalties [1].

565a2254991fe96bbbe2c039fdb24fdf0c383b21.answer:
No, not in general. A driver with a Drive-Through or Stop-and-Go Penalty may not serve it while the VSC procedure is in use or after the Safety Car has been deployed, with one exception: a driver who was already in the Pit Entry Road or Pit Lane for the purpose of serving the penalty may do so [1][3].

Any Control Line crossings a driver makes behind the Safety Car or during the VSC procedure count toward the maximum number of crossings allowed for serving the penalty [1][3].

9a052efd7d502c4b7c210181585363e0ce9bdef8.answer:
The passages don't say how long a team has to receive a decision about one of its drivers, or whether it must confirm receipt.

The closest provision is about notifying competitors of an investigation, not of a decision. Under B1.9.2, if stewards are investigating an incident, a message identifying the drivers involved must be sent to all competitors. That message must be displayed no later than 60 minutes after the end-of-session signal of a TTCS, and until it is displayed, the drivers concerned may not leave the circuit without the stewards' consent [1]. This sets a deadline for the investigation notice, not for a decision or any confirmation.

The other passages don't address this either. B1.7.3 covers the 7-day notice a competitor must give the FIA about a substitute driver [2], and B3.1.4 covers scrutineers' power to check eligibility, including up to one hour after covers are fitted or removed [3].

7fd797cf6761bf95d4447014ab5a2cf746e7ed1a.answer: Any decision or communication concerning a particular Competitor should be given to them within twenty-five (25) minutes of the decision, and receipt must be acknowledged [3]. So yes, the team must confirm it received the decision.

8caa806c89f8ab07cbfae659ef14a7b6aac55ef0.answer:
**Cars per day:** For the pre-season tests, each Competitor may use only one F1 Car on each day. This applies to both the Pre-Season Private Collective Testing [3] and the Pre-Season Public Collective Testing [3]. A separate Post-Season Test allows two F1 Cars per Competitor, but it is a single day held after the last Competition [1].

**Hours:** The passages do not specify the hours a testing day covers. The Pre-Season Public Testing refers to "running times as specified in Article B11.2.1," but that article is not included in the provided text [3]. The Private Testing passage says a day of track running counts from the moment a car first leaves the Pit Lane, but it does not give a start or end time [3].

5558efb9195033d6313e1ff5ce0a893c6ff5c877.answer:
Under the TPC (private testing) provisions, each Competitor may have no more than one car available and may use only one car on any testing day [1]. A testing day is a single continuous nine-hour period between 09:00 and 19:00 [1]. The passages don't say exactly where within that 10-hour window the nine hours must fall.

For collective testing under TCC, each Competitor may use only one F1 Car on each day [2][3].

c0b8a125b32d9131ae7503590b3f3c034d9fe653.answer:
The passages don't say that the Safety Car heads back to the pits once the leader is behind it. [1] covers how lapped cars overtake the Safety Car and how the green light is extinguished, but it doesn't address when the Safety Car returns to the pits.

The only pit-entry timing given is for the end of a race. If the Safety Car is still deployed at the beginning of the last lap, or is deployed during the last lap, it enters the Pit Lane at the end of that lap, unless the Race Director requires its continued presence after the end-of-session signal [3].

482fdeb356603179c01c66de77e10a2e29c2adba.answer:
Once the leader is behind the Safety Car, it does not return to the pits straight away. It must stay out at least until the leader is behind it and all remaining F1 Cars are queued behind it [1].

After the "LAPPED CARS MAY NOW OVERTAKE" message has been sent, the Safety Car returns to the pits at the end of the following lap, unless the Race Director considers its presence still necessary [1].

The passages also describe a separate withdrawal signal. When the Race Director decides it is safe to end the Safety Car period, the "SAFETY CAR IN THIS LAP" message is sent and the orange lights are extinguished. The Safety Car then enters the Pit Lane at the end of that lap [2].

The passages do not give the full conditions for sending the "LAPPED CARS MAY NOW OVERTAKE" message, which are in Article B5.13.4c and are not included here.

f85fc735bf99d7e064334cd297f9cfaa450a782e.answer:
A car that was in its garage when the restart was paused does not line up on the grid. It must re-enter the Pit Lane and may join the TTCS only once the Pit Lane exit is opened after the standing start resumption [2][3].

If it fails to resume the TTCS from the Pit Lane when required, a Stop-and-Go Penalty will be imposed [3]. The passages do not specify a particular position within the Pit Lane for this car.

448061aaf5382aeadde5e9deceb9cdfb34dd5509.answer:
A car that was in its garage when the restart was suspended lines up at the **back of the line of F1 Cars in the Fast Lane**, in the order it arrives there. [3]

Before it can join, the car must re-enter the Pit Lane. It may join the TTCS once the Pit Lane exit opens after the resumption. [1][2] The Safety Car is positioned at the front of the line of F1 Cars in the Fast Lane. [3]

The passages describe the Pit Lane timing slightly differently. [3] says these cars are "permitted to leave the Pit Lane at the resumption time," while [1] and [2] tie joining to the Pit Lane exit opening after the resumption.
